sweep_summary: no new first-hand stress text was read, so the catalog's tonal-OR-pitch accent coding (Kotz 1909 'Der Ton liegt meistens auf der vorletzten Silbe' + lexical Tonhöhe pairs; Kähler-Meyer 1962 via Hyman 2006: H/L tone with phrase-final penult Dehnungsakzent/Druckakzent) stands unchanged. (1) Kähler-Meyer 1963/64 'Töne und Akzente in der Formenlehre des Chasu', Afrika und Übersee 47:89-133 (two duplicate Glottolog records, 84552/176698, already in our bibliography) is the direct sequel to the 1962 tonal study and the single most likely source to refine the catalog's stress/tone statement for Chasu; it is print-only (HathiTrust Bd.47-48 umn.31951001892726b search-only, not on archive.org, no DOI) -> priority high. (2) Philippson 1991/92 thesis 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (Paris 5, 542 pp.): theses.fr abstract read (tonal-to-penult-stress continuum across c. 30 East Bantu languages, penult demarcative accent as evolutionary driver); Glottolog codes Asu among its languages; not online (theses.fr accessible=non, not in HAL) -> priority medium. (3) Philippson 2005 'Pitch accent in Comorian and Proto-Sabaki tones' (Tervuren Festschrift, pp. 199-220): Comorian/Sabaki comparative tone; Asu coded only as a comparison language; no open copy -> priority low.org, Crossref, theses.fr, Glottolog, RMCA and UGent catalogues.fr JSON, four Glottolog ref JSONs, HathiTrust holdings JSON) and a record are On-disk Kipare texts from the earlier search (Herman 1995, Kagaya 1989 scanned pages, Schlindwein 1985) were a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/accent statements: no hits.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Chasu 'tonal' on Kotz 1909 (penultimate 'Ton' plus lexical pitch distinctions) with Hyman 2006 secondary. Philippson confirms the tonal classification from first-hand data and adds an explicit, typologically framed statement that the penult bears a demarcative intensity/length prominence without pitch culmination: compatible with Kotz's 'Der Ton liegt meistens auf der vorletzten Silbe' read as penultimate stress alongside lexical tone; adds detail (four noun-stem tone classes, no length contrast, no Meeussen's rule, N vs S dialect difference in H association).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Asu (Chasu/Pare) is a tone language: four lexical tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems (LL, HL, LH, HH), H vs toneless verb radicals, one-to-one tone-to-syllable association, no Meeussen's rule, no vowel-length contrast; independently of tone, the penultimate syllable of the word carries a non-distinctive intensity accent realized as lengthening (a culmination of length, not of pitch).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect note only: in the southern dialects the H of a verb radical also associates to the extensions (Annexe item 9; ch.4 §3.1); a final H is clearly lowered after a preceding H (p.485). No exceptions to the penultimate length culmination are stated for Asu.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Asu data are his own field notes, examples 'pris dans un sous-dialecte septentrional' (North Pare), with remarks on the southern dialects (H of the radical spreading to extensions); Kähler-Meyer's article concerns Chasu of the Pare mountains (Tanganyika) generally; the catalog record rests on Kotz 1909 (Pare-Gebirge).

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated locators (Kotz 1909 p. 3 + Nachtrag p. 73; Hyman 2006:247 ex. 24 + fn. 9). (2) The record rests on a 1909 missionary grammar sketch plus a second-hand report of Kähler-Meyer 1962; that is thin sourcing for a language with a dozen dedicated tonal studies, but every better source opened now agrees with the classification: Kagaya 1989 (Gonja and Mbaga Chasu: two basic tones H/L plus downstep, TBU = vowel/syllabic nasal, no stress section), Schlindwein 1985 (lexical H/L verb radicals, downstep), Herman 1995 (instrumental: three tonal categories H, !H, L; utterance-final lowering), Odden's 1985 précis in the same SAL volume (downstep, utterance-final H register lowering). None mentions an independent word-stress rule; the utterance-final tonal effects are consistent with the phrase domain coded. Languoid identity is sound: Kaga

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 1989. A study on the tonal system of the Gonja verbs and nouns (a dialect of the Southern Pare language). In Kagaya, Besha & Yukawa (eds.), Studies in Tanzanian Languages (Bantu Linguistics (ILCAA) 2), 1-94. Tokyo: ILCAA.
sources.quote: p. 2: 'This language is called "Chasu" by its speakers. ... It turned out that each tonal pattern was represented by the high level tone, the low level tone and the downstep and that it was derived from two basic (underlying) tones (high and low) and a particular sequence of tones which causes the downstep.' p. 4: infinitives split into tonal Group I (L stems: kula, kubigha) vs Group II (H stems: kusha, kuvéna, kuréréha). No mention of stress/accent/penult in the pages read.
sources.note: 204 pp of dedicated tonal description of two Chasu (S. Pare) dialects; should replace the 1909 mission grammar as the primary open-text source for the tonal classification.

sources.citation: Kagaya, Ryohei. 1989. A study on the tonal system of the Mbaga dialect of the Southern Pare language. In Studies in Tanzanian Languages (Bantu Linguistics (ILCAA) 2), 95-204. Tokyo: ILCAA.
sources.quote: pp. 96-97: 'a lexicon item consists of a sequence of segments and a sequence of basic tones. Among segments, a vowel and a syllabic nasal m can carry a tone, thus called a tone bearing unit (TBU)'; association conventions A1-A6 with floating H/L. Table of contents is entirely tonal patterns of verbs, infinitives, imperatives, nouns, modifiers; no stress/accent section.

sources.citation: Herman, Rebecca. 1995. Final lowering in Kipare. OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 45: 36-55 (published version: Phonology 13:171-196, 1996).
sources.quote: p. 36/37: 'Kipare, a Bantu language which has both lexical tone and final lowering'; p. 38: 'all three tonal categories of Kipare, namely H, !H, and L'; speaker from Same district (Pare). Instrumental F0 study of one speaker; lowering of H -> !H and !H -> L utterance-finally (citing Odden 1986a,b). Silent on penultimate lengthening/stress; its utterance-final tonal effects are consistent with the PHRASE-level coding of final H -> L in our record.
sources.locator: Abstract p. 36; sec. 1 p. 37-38; sec. 2 p. 38
sources.note: Only instrumental (F0) study of Pare prosody; confirms three lexical tonal categories and utterance-level final lowering; citable as instrumental support for tonal + phrase-level final effects.

sources.citation: Schlindwein, Deborah. 1985. Downstep in the Kipare verb complex. Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 9 (Précis from the 15th Conference on African Linguistics), 285-289.
sources.quote: 'This paper deals with some selected aspects of the tone system of one dialect of Kipare, an Eastern Bantu language spoken in Tanzania. Kipare downstep is the phonetic realization of a floating low tone sandwiched between two high tones ... The Kipare verb radical generally consists of either one or two syllables, the first of which is lexically specified for either a high (H) or a low (L) tone.' No stress/accent/penult statement. (Same volume, Odden's tone-register précis, the text layer: Kipare has downstep but no downdrift and 'a rule assigning an utterance-final H to a lower regist
sources.note: Short open tonal précis (lexical H/L verb radicals, downstep from floating L); independent confirmation of the tonal classification.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernes a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.
sources.note: Abstract only (theses.fr). Comparative tone/accent typology of c. 30 East African Bantu languages, ranging from fully tonal (Kikuyu) to demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili); hypothesis that the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent drives the evolution of these systems. Glottolog's language coding for the thesis includes Asu (Tanzania) [asa], so Chasu is among the languages treated, but the abstract says nothing Asu-specific.
